extracted.intended_audience: Reviewers (program committee, associate chairs, and external reviewers) assessing submissions to ACM CHI 2026
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for performing peer review of submissions to the ACM CHI 2026 conference, covering evaluation criteria (contribution, originality, transparency), review content and length, confidentiality and AI-tool use, and policies on length and prior publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary criterion: contribution to HCI
rubrics_metrics.description: Does this submission provide a strong contribution to the field of HCI?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the primary criterion for all papers. There are many ways a paper can make a contribution to HCI; review the paper appropriately for its contribution type (see 'Contributions to CHI' and 'Guide to a Successful Submission'). A CHI paper must make an original research contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall recommendation must match written appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers decide the overall recommendation (Accept with minor revisions, Revise and Resubmit, and Reject) on each submission with written appraisal that matches with their recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the textual review justifies and is consistent with the chosen overall recommendation; inconsistent short comments or missing justification undermine PC decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review length and level of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: A high-quality review is typically about a page of written text; very short reviews are frustrating for authors, tend to be less constructive, and hurt the review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put yourself in the author's position: provide the level of detailed feedback you would want. Write a detailed review whether or not you like the paper — short positive or negative reviews without justification are insufficient, especially when there are well-argued counter-reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer responsibility for content and accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: As a reviewer, you are responsible for the content and accuracy of your reviews, including the references cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-check claims, references, and factual assertions in your review. Be especially careful when using external tools (including AI) that may introduce errors; inaccurate reviews can negatively reflect on the reviewer and the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining confidentiality is crucial in the review process; quoting or disclosing papers under review must be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sharing content from unpublished papers with any online tools that may store or process the data in ways that could compromise confidentiality. Copying and pasting manuscript content into third-party tools (including LLMs) may risk confidentiality and should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and prior publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Content appearing at CHI should be new and groundbreaking; material previously published in widely disseminated archival publications should not be republished unless the work has been significantly revised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant revision is roughly defined as containing more than 25% new content material (new insights, new results, etc.), though this is subjective. Exceptions: translation into English (with original author typically as author/co-author) is allowed and should be disclosed; non-archival venues (workshop presentations, posters, Late-Breaking Work) do not count as prior publication. Do not reject work because independently developed related work was published after the CHI submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication studies allowed (requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive replication of other researchers' work can be a significant contribution to HCI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitted replication work must include sufficient information to enable future replications. Efforts to include complete, well-organized supplementary material (software, analysis code, data) should be rewarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of transparency in the way research results are reported can be grounds to doubt the contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should consult the 'Transparency' section in the Guide to a Successful Submission for expectations that vary by contribution type (e.g., methods, data, analysis). Lack of clear reporting or missing details that prevent assessment or replication lowers confidence in the contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper length must be commensurate with contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper length should be commensurate with the paper's contribution; there is no arbitrary maximum or minimum, but clarity and conciseness are vital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must indicate if their paper is: short (<5,000 words), long (typically 7,000–8,000 words), or excessively long (>12,000 words). Reviewers should judge whether length is appropriate for the claimed contribution. Papers perceived as too long (repetitive/verbose) or too short (omit important details, neglect related work, or tamper with formatting) may be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short paper expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Short papers (less than 5,000 words) should present brief, focused research contributions that are noteworthy but may not be as comprehensive as long papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should not ask for more than is reasonable for a short contribution; focus on what is needed for that contribution rather than expecting the depth of a long paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessively long paper policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors of excessively long papers (more than 12,000 words) are required to justify why a shorter contribution is not suitable or not possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In very exceptional cases such submissions may be considered for full review, but only with clear, strong justification from the authors. Typical long submissions are expected to be ≈7,000–8,000 words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not penalize for imperfect subcommittee fit
rubrics_metrics.description: You should not judge the paper by how well it fits the subcommittee theme(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the paper based on its own quality; many papers will not cleanly fit into a particular subcommittee and should not be penalized for that. The subcommittee structure exists to improve reviewer matching, not to define acceptability of topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautious use of AI tools in reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of online tools (including LLM-based tools) for editing/proofreading reviews is not prohibited but must be used with care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers must understand the implications of using any tool and avoid sharing unpublished manuscript content with tools that may store or process it. LLMs can produce plausible-sounding but inaccurate outputs and often optimize for prompt completion over accuracy — reviewers are responsible for ensuring accuracy and relevance of reviews after tool use.
